\section[el desfile]{el desfile — the parade}

\label{lesson:ES-C559-desfile}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the tribute, then the Spanish for to open.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el desfile}
\textbf{el desfile} — \textquotedblleft{}the parade\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Vimos el desfile desde la ventana.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We watched the parade from the window.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Un desfile de moda} — a fashion show.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desfile} is built on \emph{desfilar} (EtymDB), from French \emph{défiler} 'to march in a line', built on \emph{fil} 'thread', from Latin \emph{fīlum}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el desfile}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el desfile}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el desfile}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the tribute, then the Spanish for to open, then say \emph{el desfile} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el desfile mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The parade\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la procesión]{la procesión — the procession}

\label{lesson:ES-C559-procesion}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to open, then the Spanish for the parade.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la procesión}
\textbf{la procesión} — \textquotedblleft{}the procession\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La procesión sale de la iglesia a las ocho.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The procession leaves the church at eight.}
\end{quote}

Very important in Holy Week, \emph{la Semana Santa}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{procesión} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{prōcessiō} 'a marching forward' (EtymDB), from \emph{prōcēdere} 'to go forward', built on \emph{cēdere} 'to go'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la procesión}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la procesión}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la procesión}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to open, then the Spanish for the parade, then say \emph{la procesión} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la procesión mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The procession\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la feria]{la feria — the fair}

\label{lesson:ES-C559-feria}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the parade, then the Spanish for the procession.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la feria}
\textbf{la feria} — \textquotedblleft{}the fair\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
En abril hay feria en Sevilla.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{In April there is a fair in Seville.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Una feria del libro} — a book fair.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{feria} is inherited from Latin \emph{fēriae} 'holidays, feast days' (EtymDB). Markets were held on feast days.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la carroza]{la carroza — the float (in a parade); the carriage}

\label{lesson:ES-C559-carroza}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the procession, then the Spanish for the fair.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la carroza}
\textbf{la carroza} — \textquotedblleft{}the float (in a parade); the carriage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Los niños saludaban desde las carrozas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The children waved from the floats.}
\end{quote}

\emph{La carroza de los Reyes Magos} — the Three Kings' float on 5 January.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{carroza} was borrowed from Italian \emph{carrozza} 'a carriage', built on \emph{carro} 'a cart', which comes from Latin \emph{carrus} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the procession, then the Spanish for the fair, then say \emph{la carroza} again

\section[la multitud]{la multitud — the crowd}

\label{lesson:ES-C559-multitud}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the fair, then the Spanish for the float.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la multitud}
\textbf{la multitud} — \textquotedblleft{}the crowd\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Una multitud esperaba en la plaza.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{A crowd was waiting in the square.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{multitud} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{multitūdō} 'a great number' (EtymDB), built on \emph{multus} 'much, many'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

(\textbf{envejecer}.) Old age? (\textbf{la vejez}.) Elderly? (\textbf{anciano}.) Death? (\textbf{la muerte}.) Dead? (\textbf{muerto}.) The deceased? (\textbf{el difunto}.) The burial? (\textbf{el entierro}.) To bury? (\textbf{enterrar}.) The wake? (\textbf{el velatorio}.) The grave? (\textbf{la tumba}.) The cemetery? (\textbf{el cementerio}.) Mourning? (\textbf{el luto}.) The death notice? (\textbf{la esquela}.) The condolences? (\textbf{el pésame}.) The coffin? (\textbf{el ataúd}.) The inheritance? (\textbf{la herencia}.) The celebration? (\textbf{la celebración}.) To celebrate? (\textbf{festejar}.) To commemorate? (\textbf{conmemorar}.) The tribute? (\textbf{el homenaje}.) To open? (\textbf{inaugurar}.) The parade? (\textbf{el desfile}.) The procession?
